t: Minimum String Length After Balanced Removals
o: We may delete any contiguous substring containing an equal number of 'a's and 'b's, then rejoin the pieces, repeating until nothing more can be removed. The key observation is that every operation removes exactly one 'a' for each 'b' it deletes, so the quantity (#a − #b) never changes — it is an invariant of the process. In "aabbab" the counts are 3 and 3, so the whole string is itself balanced and can be removed at once, giving 0. In "aaaa" there are no 'b's at all, so no balanced substring exists and the answer is 4. In "aaabb" we have #a − #b = 2, matching the expected answer of 1 leftover character after peeling off pairs like "ab". Since n ≤ 10^5, we need at most an O(n) or O(n log n) solution; anything that simulates all possible substrings naively will be too slow.
k: The difference between the count of 'a's and 'b's is invariant under every allowed removal.
Any maximal run where both letters exist can be fully reduced by repeatedly deleting adjacent opposite pairs, so only the surplus of the majority letter must remain.
Therefore the minimum final length is simply abs(count('a') - count('b')).

a.n: Approach 1: Brute-Force Simulation with a Pairing Stack
a.i: A natural first idea is to actually perform removals. Notice that any balanced substring contains at least one place where an 'a' sits next to a 'b' (adjacent in the current string), so deleting such adjacent opposite pairs one at a time is equivalent to any other removal strategy. We can simulate this with a stack: scan left to right, and whenever the incoming character is different from the top of the stack, they form a deletable "ab" or "ba" pair, so pop; otherwise push. Whatever survives on the stack cannot be paired further and its size is the answer.
s: Initialize an empty stack (or list used as a stack).
For each character c in s: if the stack is non-empty and its top differs from c, pop the top (this pair is balanced and removed).
Otherwise push c onto the stack.
After processing all characters, return the stack's size.
a.t: O(n) — each character is pushed and popped at most once.
a.sp: O(n) — the stack can hold up to all characters in the worst case (e.g., "aaaa").

a.i: Since every removal deletes equal numbers of 'a's and 'b's, the value #a − #b is invariant. Conversely, this lower bound is achievable: as long as both letters remain, some adjacent opposite pair exists somewhere in the string, and deleting such pairs repeatedly removes everything except the surplus copies of the majority letter. Hence the answer is exactly abs(#a − #b), computable in a single pass without extra memory.
s: Count how many times 'a' appears (call it ca) and how many times 'b' appears (cb).
a.t: O(n) — a single pass over the string to count characters.
a.sp: O(1) — only two counters are maintained.

w: In an interview, mention the invariant argument first — it shows deep understanding and immediately yields the one-line counting solution; the stack version is a nice way to *derive* the same result constructively and matches the problem's Stack tag. Common pitfalls: assuming you must remove substrings of even length only (any balanced substring works regardless of arrangement), or trying exponential/DP searches over all substrings. Edge cases: strings with a single distinct letter (answer = full length), already-balanced strings (answer 0), and length-1 strings (answer 1). Likely follow-ups: generalize to three letters with balanced triples, or report the actual sequence of removals rather than just the length.
